extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reviewing submissions to NeurIPS 2019: reviewer duties, how to write reviews, scoring scales, conflict/confidentiality rules, and interaction with authors/ACs during discussion and response phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reviewer will be assigned around 4-6 submissions. Reviewers are responsible for reviewing submissions, reading author responses, discussing submissions and author responses with other reviewers and area chairs (ACs), and helping make decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewing process is double blind at the level of reviewers and ACs. There are no physical meetings; discussions take place via CMT. Reviewer identities are visible to other reviewers, ACs and SACs. After decisions, reviews and meta-reviews will be made public (reviewer and SAC/AC identities remain anonymous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer best practices — availability and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: It is okay to be unavailable for part of the review process (e.g., vacation), but if unavailable for extended/important windows (discussion, decision-making) you must let your ACs know ASAP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect deadlines and respond to emails promptly. Ensure CMT email isn't blocked; keep contact details up to date. Log into TPMS and keep profile current. If you will be unavailable during critical phases, inform ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional conduct and constructive reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write thoughtful and constructive reviews that accord with the NeurIPS code of conduct. Be fair and avoid subtle discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid comments that may imply the author is 'foreign' or 'non-native'; prefer neutral formulations (example: 'Please have your submission proof-read for English style and grammar issues.'). Do not be dismissive; provide precise citations if citing prior work. Be professional and listen to other reviewers without giving in to undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep everything relating to the review process confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use ideas/results from submissions in your own work until they become public. Do not talk about or distribute submissions (or ideas/results) to anyone without prior approval from the program chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Enter domain conflicts, subject areas, TPMS info, and individual conflicts in CMT; follow NeurIPS definitions of conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you notice a conflict with an assigned submission, contact your AC immediately so the paper can be reassigned. Read this year’s conflict definitions carefully. DO NOT talk to other reviewers, ACs, or SACs about submissions assigned to you without prior approval from your AC. DO NOT talk to others about your own submissions or submissions with which you have a conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind reviewing obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing is double blind at reviewer and AC level; authors are responsible for anonymizing submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not include names, affiliations, acknowledgements, or identifying information. If a submission is not adequately anonymized, contact the corresponding AC. Do not attempt to find author identities (e.g., via Google or arXiv); if you accidentally discover identities, inform your AC and do not divulge them or let identities influence your decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary material policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may submit up to 100MB of supplementary material (PDF or ZIP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are responsible for reading the submission itself; looking at supplementary material is discretionary. Because NeurIPS submissions are short, reviewers may wish to consult supplementary material before criticizing missing details, proofs, or experimental results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are limited to eight content pages (including figures/tables) in the NeurIPS 'submission' style; additional pages containing only references are allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must use the NeurIPS 2019 LaTeX style file. If assigned submissions violate style or page limits (e.g., decreased margins or font size), contact the program chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions identical or substantially similar to papers submitted to/accepted at/published elsewhere (including other NeurIPS submissions) should be deemed dual submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slicing contributions too thinly can make submissions dual. If you suspect a dual submission or need clarification, contact the corresponding AC and program chairs. See the Call for Papers for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review content — overall guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Make reviews detailed and informative; short or superficial reviews that venture uninformed opinions are worse than no review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review content informs ACs/SACs/program chairs and helps authors improve. Reviews for accepted papers help with camera-ready improvements. Include specific, constructive critique and avoid vague subjective complaints. Don't review based on your level of interest but on scientific contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions (review form item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Please list three things this paper contributes (theoretical, methodological, algorithmic, empirical, bridging fields, critical analysis). For each, briefly state the level of significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot think of three things, explain why. Not all good papers have three contributions (e.g., a key theorem may be the main contribution). Provide polite phrasing if you judge low significance (example provided). See 'Examples of Review Content' for sample contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed comments (summary + four evaluation criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a thorough review including originality, quality, clarity, and significance. Begin by summarizing the main ideas and relating them to previous work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizing helps reveal misunderstandings. Then list strengths and weaknesses focusing on originality, quality, clarity, and significance. Be detailed, specific, and polite; avoid vague complaints. Provide complete citations where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether tasks or methods are new and whether the work novelly combines known techniques; clarify differences from previous contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check related work citations and whether the submission clearly distinguishes itself. Examples and sample critiques are provided in guideline examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (technical soundness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission technically sound? Are claims supported by theory or experiments? Is the work complete or in-progress? Are authors honest about strengths/weaknesses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify technical errors, missing experiments, or unjustified claims. Examples show how to point out technical and experimental shortcomings with specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission clearly written and well organized? Does it adequately inform the reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest constructive improvements to make the paper reproducible by an expert reader. Give concrete examples of unclear passages or notation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results important? Will others use or build on these ideas? Does it advance the state of the art or provide unique resources/approaches?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider potential impact on researchers/practitioners, difficulty of task addressed, and demonstrable improvements over previous work. Examples illustrate modest vs. high significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score (1–10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign an overall score reflecting assessment of contributions, with explicit descriptors for scores 1–10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale provided with detailed labels/examples: 10 = Top 5% of accepted NeurIPS papers (groundbreaking); 9 = Top 15% (excellent); 8 = Top 50% (very good); 7 = good; 6 = marginally above threshold; 5 = marginally below; 4 = okay but not good enough; 3 = clear reject; 2 = strong reject; 1 = trivial/wrong/already known. Do NOT adjust scores to match conference acceptance rate — score each submission on its own merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report how certain you are about your assessment using a 1–5 scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 = absolutely certain (very familiar with related work); 4 = confident but not certain; 3 = fairly confident (some parts may be unchecked); 2 = willing to defend but likely unfamiliar with central parts; 1 = educated guess (not in area or hard to understand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements (what would increase your score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain what authors would have to do in rebuttal or revision to increase your overall score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete actions (e.g., add comparisons to baselines X,Y,Z; include additional dataset; relax theorem assumptions; clarify differences from prior work; improve organization/clarity). This field can guide the author response and revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility checklist usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: State whether the Reproducibility Checklist answers were useful for evaluating the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses to the checklist will not be used to determine acceptance but could inform future NeurIPS policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code submission influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate whether code was submitted and if it influenced your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is informational and will not be used to determine acceptance but may inform future policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior review / area chairing of this work
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate whether you have previously reviewed or area chaired a version of this work for another archival venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yes/no; useful to ACs/SACs for context when interpreting the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seen online (e.g., arXiv) disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate whether you have seen this submission online (arXiv, personal website, social media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yes/no; informs ACs/SACs that the review may not have been double blind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential comments to area chair
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the confidential comments field for remarks to the AC that you do not want shared with authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May include explicit comparisons to other submissions or blunt criticisms. Use this field for sensitive content; be honest but professional. If you learned author identities accidentally, tell your AC here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response — reviewer obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors have an opportunity to respond to reviews. Reviewers must read author responses and, if appropriate, update reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore author responses. Even if your assessment remains the same, explain why it remains the same and what the author response failed to address. Keep an open mind and consider whether you overlooked something.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion phase and consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: After author responses, AC will initiate a discussion to encourage reviewers to reach consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consensus is taken seriously; unanimous assessments are rarely overruled. Discussion is important for borderline or conflicting reviews. Consider other reviewers' perspectives and change your mind if appropriate, but you are not required to. Aim for reasoned argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of review content (illustrative guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide provides many concrete examples of good/bad review content and sample reviewer comments across contributions, quality, clarity, originality, and significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples to calibrate level of detail, tone, and specificity. Examples include suggested phrasing for contributions, concrete technical critique excerpts, clarity/organization suggestions, and balanced pros/cons lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer evaluation and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs will evaluate the quality of each review with three scores: 'exceeded expectations', 'met expectations', and 'failed to meet expectations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top ~400 reviewers with highest scores receive free NeurIPS registrations; next ~2000 have registrations reserved; lowest-scoring reviewers may not be invited next year. This is an incentive to produce high-quality reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online submission system (CMT) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: All reviews must be submitted via the NeurIPS 2019 CMT site; you may revise reviews as often as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same email for author and reviewer roles if applicable. Watch for CMT emails in spam and whitelist email@msr-cmt.org. Contact program chairs (not their personal emails) when needed.
